domain: History of Mathematics / Philosophy of Mathematics / Conceptual History
topic_summary: Analysis of zero's entry into Western mathematics as a number, examining the transition from Indian/Arabic numeral systems through Fibonacci's Liber Abaci (1202) to gradual European adoption. The core tension is philosophical: Parmenidean resistance to 'nothing' as existent versus practical utility in commerce and calculation. This is flagged as a contested kernel case—the seam between zero-as-placeholder and zero-as-number.

key_entities: Brahmagupta (7th century Indian mathematician, established zero arithmetic rules)
Fibonacci/Leonardo of Pisa (1202 Liber Abaci author, Western transmitter)
Gerbert of Aurillac/Pope Sylvester II (980s early European transmitter)
Parmenides (5th century BC Greek philosopher, 'nothing cannot exist' doctrine)
Hindu-Arabic numeral system (positional notation with zero)
key_tensions: Parmenidean ontology (nothing cannot exist) vs zero-as-number (nothing as mathematical entity)
Greek geometric mathematics (magnitudes only) vs Indian arithmetic (operations on absence)
Roman numeral incumbency vs Arabic numeral efficiency (14th-15th century Italy)
Placeholder utility vs number status (notational convenience vs ontological commitment)
key_mechanisms: Translation transmission: al-Khwārizmī's Algoritmo de Numero Indorum (12th century Latin) as conduit
Commercial adoption: Italian merchant bookkeeping driving gradual acceptance despite resistance
Printing press diffusion: 15th century technology enabling spread beyond Northern Italy
key_absences: No discussion of negative numbers (which faced similar ontological resistance)
Limited treatment of zero's role in calculus/limits (17th century mathematical revolution)
